disclaimer: Competitor ratings are a point-in-time reading of public product documentation, the GitHub MCP listings supplied with this review, and each vendor's own words. Products change; every cell therefore carries a basis and an accessible note, and any cell the review could not evidence is marked 'unknown' instead of guessed. TestForge's own column is not marketing: each 'yes' is a claim with machine-checkable evidence (file, symbol, route or test) that GET /api/market/audit re-verifies on demand and in CI. Run the audit before quoting this matrix to anyone.

groups.name: Discovery and verified defects
groups.blurb: Does the tool find defects nobody scripted, prove them, and hand over evidence a human or CI can trust?

groups.name: Authoring and reuse
groups.blurb: How tests are created, reused, searched and repaired over time.

groups.name: Application coverage
groups.blurb: Which interfaces and application types the tool can actually drive.

groups.name: API and contract quality
groups.blurb: Testing the service layer rather than only the pixels.

groups.name: AI agents and MCP interoperability
groups.blurb: Whether the tool can be driven by, or drive, an AI client without lock-in.

groups.name: CI gates and release decisions
groups.blurb: Everything that decides whether a build may ship: determinism, machine-readable results, impact analysis.

groups.name: Trust, operations and cost
groups.blurb: Licence, hosting, privacy, access control and the ability to keep running when a vendor or a model does not.

groups.name: Reporting and integration
groups.blurb: What a stakeholder, an auditor or a ticketing system receives.

capabilities.name: Finds unknown bugs without a script
capabilities.why: A scripted suite can only fail where somebody already wrote an expectation. Discovery of unscripted defects is the capability that separates QA from replay.

self.note: app/explorer.py crawls a black-box URL with deterministic checks (HTTP 4xx/5xx, console errors, broken images, missing accessible names, duplicate ids, empty-form validation, slow responses) and files findings. It is rule-based exploration, not an LLM reasoning loop, so it will not invent business-logic scenarios.

notes.argus: The listing's headline claim: autonomously finds unknown bugs (screenshot row 1).
notes.playwright-mcp: No: documented as a driver for an LLM's actions, not a bug finder.
notes.chrome-devtools-mcp: No: a debugger/inspector for an AI client.
notes.browser-use: Partial and task-scoped: it completes the objective it is given and scores its own result.
notes.testrigor: Partial: generative AI drafts tests from plain English, which still needs a human to state the intent.
notes.testatlas: No: maps an existing solution; it does not explore for defects.
notes.playwright: No: a driver and runner; discovery is the user's code.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented in this release as deterministic, zero-LLM discovery: reproducible rules, verified findings and receipts. LLM-authored exploratory scenarios are explicitly out of scope so the gate stays deterministic.

capabilities.name: Independently verifies each finding
capabilities.why: An unverified finding wastes engineering time and destroys trust in the tool. Verification must be repeatable and must not be the same model scoring itself.

self.note: Every explorer finding is re-checked on a second and third pass and only marked verified when the same condition reproduces; the receipt records attempts, timestamps and a SHA-256 over the finding body. Rules agents (failure triage, flaky analysis) also carry their signals so a human can re-derive the call.

notes.argus: The listing claims each finding is independently verified and a receipt is produced (screenshot row 2).
notes.browser-use: No on independent verification: the same LLM loop scores its own outcome.
notes.testatlas: No: it maps an existing solution; it verifies bindings, not defects.
notes.playwright: No: assertions verify a written expectation, not an independent re-check of a new finding.
notes.applitools: No: matches a baseline somebody approved.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented in this release: deterministic re-check with a reproducible receipt.

capabilities.name: Evidence-rich bug report
capabilities.why: A defect a developer cannot reproduce is a conversation, not a fix. The report needs URL, steps, expected/actual, status codes and logs.

self.note: Explorer findings carry the URL, the check that failed, captured console/network signals, bounded DOM evidence and replayable steps; app/qa_agents/defects.py renders Jira-ready markdown, Jira wiki and a CSV row, and app/report_routes.py attaches per-step screenshots to the HTML report.

notes.browser-use: Partial: a screenshot and a final answer, not a defect dossier.
notes.playwright-mcp: No: raw page state and tool output.
notes.testrigor: Partial: dashboards and reports are advertised without a defect dossier.
notes.applitools: Partial: visual diffs and batch reports, not a full defect narrative.
notes.playwright: No: reporters emit test results, not a defect report.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability, extended with explorer findings and the JUnit/JSON result files.

capabilities.name: Works black-box (no repo access)
capabilities.why: Most testers do not own the system under test. A tool that needs the source cannot test a vendor product, an acquired system or somebody else's API.

self.note: Recording, replay, assertions, batching, explorer and the QA agents all need a URL, credentials or pasted text. Source access is never required.

notes.testatlas: No: static analysis needs the solution and a .NET toolchain.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: Reproduction receipt for every finding
capabilities.why: A receipt makes a finding auditable after the fact: what ran, when, against which build, and whether it still reproduces.

self.note: Explorer receipts carry a content hash, attempt count, timestamps and target build label; deterministic pilots mint a 24-hour receipt (app/support_matrix.py) and library publication writes push receipts (app/library_store.py).

notes.argus: The listing names the verification artefact a receipt (screenshot row 2).
notes.chrome-devtools-mcp: Partial: DevTools traces and performance recordings are strong evidence, but not a verification receipt.
notes.browser-use: No: the agent re-runs only when asked and scores itself.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented in this release for discovery findings; run receipts already existed.

capabilities.name: Failure triage and ownership
capabilities.why: A failure that is not classified becomes a group chat. Product, automation, data and environment failures belong to different people.

self.note: app/qa_agents/triage.py classifies every failure as product, automation, data or environment with a confidence score and the signals behind it; the executor's retry buckets only decide retries and are unchanged.

notes.mabl: Partial: failure classification and auto-healing are advertised with the vendor's ML, without published signal-level explanation.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: Record and replay authoring
capabilities.why: Most testers are not programmers. Recording captures the real interaction and makes it repeatable.

self.note: app/recorder.py records browser and Windows desktop sessions; app/executor.py replays them step by step with live preview, retries and evidence.

notes.playwright: Partial: codegen produces a script that must then be maintained.
notes.cypress: Partial: the runner records video and time-travels, but authoring is code.
notes.argus: Not stated in the supplied listing.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: Portable code export
capabilities.why: Nobody should be trapped in a recorder. Export to code the team already owns and the tool can be replaced.

self.note: app/export_formats.py emits Python and JavaScript Playwright, Gherkin, JSON execution plans, Jira/Azure/TestComplete workbooks and a runnable project skeleton (app/export_templates.py).

notes.playwright: Partial: it is the target language, not an exporter from a recording UI.
notes.testatlas: Yes per the README: Gherkin features, step definitions and a dependency map are committed outputs.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: Reusable step catalogue and phrase resolution
capabilities.why: Duplicated step wording is the main reason automation suites rot. Reuse-first authoring answers 'does this already exist?' before a new step is written.

self.note: app/step_catalog.py builds a deterministic catalogue from the stored library: normalised action, placeholder pattern, allowed values, the recordings that use it, and a resolve_step answer of bound, ambiguous or unbound with ranked candidates.

notes.testatlas: Yes: resolve_step and step_catalog are named outputs in the supplied README.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented in this release for the TestForge library.

capabilities.name: Search across existing tests
capabilities.why: Search is how a tester avoids writing the fifth version of the same login step.

self.note: GET /api/steps/search runs a bounded, deterministic ranked search over step labels, actions, URLs and recording names; GET /api/library already lists the catalogue. No index server and no LLM needed.

notes.testatlas: Yes: SQLite FTS5 over step definitions and scenarios per the README.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented in this release.

capabilities.name: Self-healing locators
capabilities.why: UI churn is the top maintenance cost of browser automation. Healing must be explainable, not a silent guess.

self.note: The recorder captures structured, stable attributes (test id, role, accessible name, id, name) and replay reports an explicit ambiguity instead of clicking the first unrelated match; there is no scored candidate-healing engine yet, so this stays partial.

notes.playwright: Partial: strict-mode ambiguity errors and user-written fallbacks, not automatic healing.
notes.testatlas: Partial: reports ambiguous bindings instead of repairing steps.

capabilities.roadmap: Roadmap: scored multi-candidate healing with an audit trail of every healed locator. Not claimed until it exists.

capabilities.name: Visual regression and baselines
capabilities.why: Layout, overlap and rendering defects pass DOM assertions. Visual baselines catch them.

self.note: app/visual_regression.py stores a promoted baseline per recording, step and viewport and compares it with a bounded Pillow diff: per-pixel luminance delta, a tolerance that absorbs JPEG re-encode noise, a changed-pixel ratio, the mean delta and the bounding box of the change. app/visual_routes.py promotes a run's step evidence (POST /api/visual/baselines), compares a run against it (POST /api/visual/compare) and returns a pass/fail verdict per step with both content hashes. Deliberately not included, and not claimed: no AI ignore-regions, no cross-browser baseline matrix and no auto-healing - a baseline changes only when a human promotes a new one.

notes.applitools: Yes: visual AI comparison is the product.
notes.playwright: Partial: toHaveScreenshot with baselines is built in, with human review of diffs.
notes.mabl: Yes: visual change detection is advertised.

capabilities.roadmap: Shipped: the deterministic baseline store and the bounded Pillow diff from this roadmap, on the same evidence contract. Applitools and mabl still lead on visual AI ignore-regions and cross-browser baseline matrices, which are out of scope here.

capabilities.name: Accessibility checks
capabilities.why: Accessible UIs are testable UIs: roles and labels are also the most stable automation locators.

self.note: The explorer flags missing accessible names and duplicate ids, and the requirement and code-review agents flag missing accessibility criteria and fragile selectors. There is no WCAG rule engine or conformance report, so this is partial only.

notes.mabl: Yes: accessibility checks are an advertised feature.
notes.playwright: Partial: axe integration is available in the ecosystem, not built in.

capabilities.roadmap: Roadmap: a WCAG 2.2 rule subset with per-page evidence and a conformance summary. Explorer signal collection is implemented now.

capabilities.name: Data-driven runs
capabilities.why: One flow must prove many rows: boundaries, invalid data and locale variants.

self.note: Execution plans carry typed datasets (CSV/JSON upload, per-row overrides, precedence rules) and the plan runner reports per-row results (app/plan_runtime.py).

notes.playwright: Partial: data comes from user code and fixtures, not a managed dataset.
notes.testatlas: Partial: datasets are part of Gherkin scenarios it maps, not a managed runner feature.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: Multi-browser engines
capabilities.why: Chromium-only coverage misses WebKit and Gecko behaviour, including the bugs that only affect Safari users.

self.note: The execution matrix records a browser per profile, but the runner launches Chromium only. Firefox and WebKit are not yet selectable, and the docs say so.

notes.playwright: Yes: Chromium, Firefox and WebKit from one API.
notes.cypress: Partial: Chromium-family and Firefox in the open-source runner; WebKit needs paid Cloud.
notes.chrome-devtools-mcp: No by design: it drives Chrome.

capabilities.roadmap: Roadmap R13 from the Playwright gap review: engine selection, install strategy and engine recorded in results.

capabilities.name: Windows desktop automation
capabilities.why: ERP and legacy business systems still open a WinForms, WPF or MFC window.

self.note: app/desktop_runner.py provides a bounded sequential UIA adapter with a deterministic simulator and an authenticated Windows agent bridge. Live control requires TF_WINDOWS_AGENT_URL/TOKEN, and the Support Matrix badges it SIMULATOR READY rather than verified.

notes.testrigor: Yes: desktop (and mainframe) coverage is advertised.
notes.selenium: Partial: WinAppDriver exists but is a separate project and is no longer actively maintained by Microsoft.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented simulator-first; live Windows agent needed for a real target.

capabilities.name: Native mobile and rugged devices
capabilities.why: Warehouse, field and consumer flows are mobile-first; a browser-only QA tool cannot see them.

self.note: app/mobile_runner.py covers Android (UiAutomator2), iOS (XCUITest) and Zebra DataWedge scanning through a simulator or an authenticated Appium hub bridge. No real device is claimed without a configured hub.

notes.selenium: Partial: Appium is a separate project built on the WebDriver protocol.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented simulator-first; live hub needed for a real device.

capabilities.name: ERP/CRM domain packs
capabilities.why: Enterprise QA teams spend most of their time in Oracle, SAP, Salesforce and Dynamics, where locators and frames are hostile.

self.note: Seven packs (Oracle, SAP Fiori, JD Edwards, Dynamics 365 F&O and Business Central, Odoo, Salesforce) run against a deterministic local fixture with positive/negative datasets and teardown resets. This is not vendor certification and no real tenant is claimed.

notes.katalon: Partial: ERP testing is served by generic keyword/record features rather than shipped domain packs.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented packs; a real tenant pilot is customer work.

capabilities.name: Frames, iframes and popups
capabilities.why: Enterprise apps nest iframes and open popups; a runner that cannot switch context cannot test them.

self.note: A step addresses nested frames through a saved CSS frame chain of up to five selectors, validated at authoring time and honoured by both the Python replay runtime and the exported JavaScript runtime; a popup is opened with a page alias and switched back to by name; and evidence masking walks every frame before a screenshot is written. Not claimed: automatic frame discovery during recording - the chain is authored, not inferred from a session.

evidence.contains: frames must contain at most five

notes.cypress: Partial: iframe support has historically needed workarounds; popups are constrained.

capabilities.roadmap: Shipped: saved frame chains and popup aliases (R05). The remaining gap is inferring the chain while recording instead of authoring it.

capabilities.name: Uploads and downloads
capabilities.why: Invoice, statement and document flows are upload/download flows.

self.note: upload_file carries an inline fixture whose filename, MIME type and base64 payload are all validated and size-capped, and download asserts the suggested filename, enforces the 512 KiB evidence cap and saves the artefact into the run directory. Both steps exist in the Python replay runtime and in the exported JavaScript runtime, and the recorder's own resource downloads and artifact ZIPs still work as before. Not claimed: assertions on the bytes of a downloaded file - the step contract compares name and size, not content.

notes.playwright: Yes: file chooser, setInputFiles and download events are first-class.

capabilities.roadmap: Shipped: user-authored upload fixtures and download assertions (R04). The remaining gap is content-level assertions on a downloaded file (checksum or parsed body).

capabilities.name: Network mocking and request control
capabilities.why: Deterministic tests need to force the 500, the timeout and the empty response without waiting for a real outage.

self.note: mock_route installs a scoped route with a fulfilled status, body and content type - or an abort - and clear_routes removes every mock the recording installed, so a mock cannot leak into the next test. Both are capped at ten live mocks per recording and validated at authoring time (bounded URL pattern, HTTP status range, response size). Implemented in the Python replay runtime and in the exported JavaScript runtime, and covered by tests in both. Not claimed: HAR replay and automatic mock recording from a live session.

notes.playwright: Yes: page.route with fulfill/abort and HAR replay.

capabilities.roadmap: Shipped: scoped mocks that never leak between tests (R06). The remaining gap is HAR replay and recording mocks from a live session, neither of which is claimed.

capabilities.name: HTTP/API testing
capabilities.why: Half the defects live behind the UI, and API checks are cheaper and more stable than clicking.

self.note: The step contract has a first-class api_request step: method, headers, body, expected status, a JSON path with an expected value and a captured variable, bounded by the same 512 KiB cap as file evidence and validated at authoring time. It runs in the Python replay runtime and in the exported JavaScript runtime, and Postman collections import straight into it. The API contract agent still reviews OpenAPI/Swagger specs and drafts contract tests on top of it.

notes.playwright: Yes: APIRequestContext is a built-in HTTP client with assertions.

capabilities.roadmap: Shipped: HTTP steps with bounded status/header/JSON assertions and captured values (R06). Not claimed: a full Postman-style collection runner with environments and scripts.

capabilities.name: API contract review
capabilities.why: A missing 401, an echoed stack trace or an unbounded payload is cheapest to catch in the spec, before a single request runs.

self.note: app/qa_agents/api_contract.py reviews OpenAPI 3 and Swagger 2 (JSON or YAML) for validation, security and error-contract gaps and drafts executable contract tests.

notes.mabl: Partial: API testing is supported; a spec review is not a named feature.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: MCP server (AI-client interoperability)
capabilities.why: MCP is how an AI client reaches a tool. A server means no lock-in to one vendor's assistant.

self.note: app/qa_agents/mcp_server.py speaks JSON-RPC over stdio with no SDK dependency and exposes the nine agents, stored-data sources, market position, gaps, step resolution and impact analysis. Read-only tools never start a browser or change data.

notes.argus: Yes: distributed as an MCP server.
notes.testatlas: Yes: 'all of it served to an AI agent over stdio' per the README.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability, extended in this release.

capabilities.name: QA agent hub (requirements to defects)
capabilities.why: Teams want AI help across the whole lifecycle, not only at authoring time, and they need the rules to work when no model is available.

self.note: Nine agents (requirements, test cases, API contract, code review, triage, flaky analysis, defect drafting, regression selection, release summary) run a deterministic rules engine always and add AI insights only when a provider key exists.

notes.argus: Partial: autonomous QA and verification, not a nine-agent lifecycle hub.
notes.testatlas: Partial: a static code map served to an agent.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: Requirements review and case generation
capabilities.why: Most escaped defects start as an ambiguous requirement. Reviewing the words is cheaper than testing the code.

self.note: Requirement Review finds missing acceptance criteria, vague terms, unhandled edges and open questions; Test Case Generation produces positive, negative and boundary cases with a Jira/Azure-ready CSV and Gherkin.

notes.testrigor: Partial: generates tests from plain-English intent; it does not review the requirement.
notes.testatlas: Partial: maps existing Gherkin rather than authoring it.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: Zero-LLM, deterministic CI gate
capabilities.why: A gate must return the same verdict for the same build. Model temperature has no place in a release decision.

self.note: Replay, assertions, triage and all nine agents have a rules mode; batch runs are deterministic and sequential, JUnit XML and JSON results are emitted, and the market claim audit plus the pilot suite fail the build on drift. AI insights are additive and never required.

notes.playwright: Yes: the runner and assertions are deterministic; gates are composed from its exit code and reporters.
notes.browser-use: Partial: the loop depends on a model, so results are not reproducible by construct.
notes.testatlas: Partial: deterministic analysis, but it is not a run gate.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented in this release: JUnit XML, JSON results, the claim audit and the pilot receipt are all model-free.

capabilities.name: CI integration out of the box
capabilities.why: A tool that cannot be called from a pipeline is a manual chore.

self.note: tools/tf.py is the packaged runner: `tf run --plan nightly.json --wait --junit results.xml --json report.json` queues a run or a batch over the existing API, polls until it is terminal, collects the JUnit XML and the JSON report, and exits 0 for a pass, 1 for a failed suite and 2 for a pipeline mistake. Standard library only, so it runs on any CI image with Python 3.9+. Alongside it: batch runs, Jenkinsfile export, GitHub workflows, JSON/JUnit/PDF report endpoints and a documented Docker path. Not claimed: vendor-specific CI apps or hosted dashboards.

notes.playwright: Yes: first-class GitHub Actions and sharding support.

capabilities.roadmap: Shipped: `tf run --plan` (plus status, junit and report) over the existing API. Not claimed: a first-party GitHub Action or a hosted CI dashboard.

capabilities.name: Machine-readable results (JUnit/JSON)
capabilities.why: Every CI system and every dashboard speaks JUnit or JSON. Screenshots alone cannot gate a pipeline.

self.note: app/ci_results.py renders deterministic JUnit XML (suites, cases, failures, skipped, timings, escaped text) for a single run or a batch, alongside the existing JSON run report and batch report.

notes.selenium: Partial: reporting is delegated to the runner or framework around it.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented in this release.

capabilities.name: Impact analysis and blast radius
capabilities.why: Running everything is slow; running nothing is negligent. Change-to-test mapping is the only way to be both fast and safe.

self.note: app/impact_map.py builds a deterministic dependency graph from stored projects and recordings (URLs, step labels, selectors, actions) and answers which tests a changed file, route or label reaches, with the reason for each edge and a ready batch payload.

notes.testatlas: Yes: blast radius across a .NET solution is a headline capability in the supplied README.
notes.playwright: Partial: --only-changed needs user-built mapping.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented in this release over the TestForge library graph.

capabilities.name: Flaky detection and analysis
capabilities.why: Flaky tests train teams to ignore red builds, which then hides real failures.

self.note: app/qa_agents/flaky.py computes flip rate, timing ratio, repeated error clusters and time-of-day patterns from run history, and ranks root causes; the plan runner keeps the stricter 'passed on retry = flaky' status.

notes.playwright: Partial: retries are configurable and reporters expose the flaky outcome, without root-cause analysis.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: Bounded parallel execution
capabilities.why: Suite duration decides how often teams can ship. Parallelism must be bounded to the machine that pays for it.

self.note: app/bounded_pool.py and app/run_pool.py give every execution unit a bounded, fair, cancellable slot: single runs and whole batches share one pool whose width is TF_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS clamped by the browser budget (TF_MAX_BROWSERS), slots are handed out in submission order, cancel_all stops in-flight work and never starts the rest, and the width defaults to 1 so the hosted instance stays exactly as sequential as it always was. Partial, not yes: the recordings inside one batch are still replayed one at a time, so a single suite does not get shorter unless it is split across runs.

notes.playwright: Yes: workers and sharding are built in.

capabilities.roadmap: Part shipped (R14): the bounded pool, global resource control and fair cancellation exist, and sequential is still the default. Still open: replaying the recordings of one batch in parallel, each in its own context, with the memory guard deciding the real ceiling.

capabilities.name: Release go/no-go report
capabilities.why: Somebody has to sign the release. A generated verdict with the evidence beats a slide built by hand.

self.note: app/qa_agents/release.py writes a stakeholder release summary with a go/no-go recommendation from the latest result of every test, known defects and open risks; PDF and HTML per-run reports supply the evidence.

notes.mabl: Partial: dashboards and quality signals, with the judgement left to the team.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: Free and open source
capabilities.why: Cost and lock-in decide what a QA team can adopt without a procurement cycle.

self.note: Apache-2.0, no per-seat or per-run pricing, no vendor account required.

notes.argus: Free MCP listing; confirm the upstream licence before redistribution.
notes.cypress: Partial: the runner is MIT, the useful parallel/dashboard features are paid.
notes.katalon: Partial: free tier with paid seats and add-ons.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing position.

capabilities.name: Self-hosted and offline-capable
capabilities.why: Regulated and air-gapped environments cannot send data to a vendor cloud.

self.note: Runs from Docker/Compose with SQLite or your Postgres. The rules engine, replay, reports, explorer, step catalogue and impact map need no outbound model call; AI is opt-in via one environment variable.

notes.cypress: Partial: the OSS runner is local, the collaboration layer is Cloud.
notes.argus: Partial: the server is local, but the AI client supplies the reasoning.
notes.katalon: Partial: Studio is local; TestOps can be self-hosted on paid plans.
notes.testrigor: No: vendor cloud (private cloud on request).
notes.applitools: No: Eyes cloud and account are required.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing position.

capabilities.name: Secret redaction in evidence
capabilities.why: Reports and screenshots leak credentials more often than breaches do. Redaction has to be the default.

self.note: app/qa_agents/common.py scrubs passwords, tokens, keys, connection strings and e-mails from every agent input and output; app/errors.py redacts errors; app/evidence.py masks password fields and known secret values before encoding screenshots.

notes.katalon: Partial: secure storage for credentials, without evidence-level masking guarantees.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.

capabilities.name: Access control and RBAC
capabilities.why: QA data contains production credentials and customer data. Single-tenant demos are not a security model.

self.note: app/access_control.py provides one operator token with signed sessions, rate-limited login and a health signal that says when the instance is unprotected. There is no multi-user RBAC or SSO, and the docs say so.

notes.mabl: Yes: SSO and workspace roles are standard SaaS controls.

capabilities.roadmap: Roadmap: SSO/RBAC with per-project roles. The single-token gate stays as the secure default.

capabilities.name: Scaling and capacity controls
capabilities.why: A tool that falls over at 200 tests is a pilot, not a platform.

self.note: Postgres read replicas, PgBouncer, a bounded shared cache, image sharding, a run queue with hygiene and explicit per-endpoint caps exist (app/db_replicas.py, app/cache.py, app/run_queue.py, app/guardrails.py). Execution itself stays one browser per instance, so throughput scales by instance, not by worker.

notes.testatlas: Partial: a local analysis tool, with no execution fleet to scale.

capabilities.roadmap: Implemented controls; worker parallelism is R14.

capabilities.name: Audit trail and provenance
capabilities.why: An auditor asks who changed what, what ran against which build, and whether the report is the one that was produced.

self.note: Run step logs carry timestamps and outcomes; library publication writes receipts with commit SHAs; pilot and claim audits carry expiry and hashes. There is no append-only, tamper-evident audit log yet.

notes.katalon: Yes: TestOps keeps execution history and audit views.

capabilities.roadmap: Roadmap: append-only event log with hash chaining for run and configuration changes.

capabilities.name: Self-contained HTML and PDF reports
capabilities.why: A report has to open on a manager's laptop with no server, no account and no network.

self.note: Per-run HTML with embedded screenshots and a strict CSP, PDF via reportlab, batch reports, and this market matrix itself exports as a standalone HTML or Markdown document from the API.

notes.testatlas: Partial: an HTML drill-down report is advertised; PDF is not named.
notes.playwright: Partial: the HTML reporter is built in, PDF needs user code.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability, extended in this release.

capabilities.name: Video and trace artefacts
capabilities.why: A failing step is explained in seconds by a video or a trace, and in hours by a log.

self.note: Runs record video where the capture policy allows and per-step screenshots are capped and masked; a Playwright trace archive is not produced.

notes.playwright: Yes: trace viewer with snapshots, network and console.

capabilities.roadmap: Roadmap: optional trace.zip per failed run with a bounded size and a viewer link.

capabilities.name: Test-management and ticketing export
capabilities.why: Results that never reach Jira or Azure DevOps are retyped by somebody, and retyping loses evidence.

self.note: Jira, Azure DevOps and TestComplete CSV and Excel workbooks, defect drafts in Jira wiki and Markdown, a step-per-row export and a Jira-ready CSV from case generation.

notes.katalon: Yes: native Jira/Azure DevOps integrations in TestOps.
notes.testatlas: Partial: exports a feature/step map rather than results.

capabilities.roadmap: Existing capability.
